Methylmercury ($CH_3Hg^+$) binds tightly to the sulfhydryl group of cysteine, forming a complex that structurally mimics the essential amino acid L-methionine, thereby tricking the L-type neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1) into actively transporting it across the blood-brain and placental barriers, validating statement C. Minamata disease was caused by industrial discharges of inorganic and methylmercury into Minamata Bay, leading to severe bioaccumulation in fish and crippling sensory constriction, tremors, and ataxia in the human population, validating statement D.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The industrial manufacture of the anti-inflammatory drug ibuprofen ($C_{13}H_{18}O_2$, molar mass $206.3\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) is a benchmark case in green chemistry. The classic Boots process requires six stoichiometric steps with an Atom Economy of only $40.0\%$. The BHC Company green route synthesizes ibuprofen in three catalytic steps: (Step 1) Isobutylbenzene ($C_{10}H_{14}$, $134.2\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) $+ C_4H_6O_3$ ($102.1\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) $\xrightarrow{HF} C_{12}H_{16}O + CH_3COOH$ ($60.1\text{ g mol}^{-1}$); (Step 2) Hydrogenation with Raney Ni: $C_{12}H_{16}O + H_2$ ($2.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) $\to$ alcohol; (Step 3) Carbonylation with Pd catalyst: alcohol $+ CO$ ($28.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) $\to C_{13}H_{18}O_2$. Determine the percentage Atom Economy ($AE$) of this BHC catalytic process if the co-product acetic acid generated in Step 1 is not recycled, rounded to the nearest integer.
questions.explanation: Atom Economy is defined as: $AE = \frac{\text{Molar mass of desired product}}{\sum \text{Molar mass of all stoichiometric reactants}} \times 100\%$. The target product is ibuprofen ($C_{13}H_{18}O_2$), which has a molar mass of $206.3\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Summing the stoichiometric reactants across all three steps: Isobutylbenzene ($C_{10}H_{14} = 134.2\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) $+$ Acetic anhydride ($C_4H_6O_3 = 102.1\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) $+$ Hydrogen gas ($H_2 = 2.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) $+$ Carbon monoxide ($CO = 28.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$). The total mass of reactants is: $M_{\text{reactants}} = 134.2 + 102.1 + 2.0 + 28.0 = 266.3\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Substituting these molar values into the Atom Economy equation: $AE = \frac{206.3\text{ g mol}^{-1}}{266.3\text{ g mol}^{-1}} \times 100\% = 77.469\%$. Rounding to the nearest whole integer gives $77$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the springtime Antarctic stratosphere, catalytic ozone destruction proceeds primarily through the Molina chlorine monoxide dimer cycle: (1) $2ClO^\bullet + M \xrightarrow{k_1} ClOOCl + M$ (rate-determining step), followed by rapid photolysis and halogen atom recycling: (2) $ClOOCl + h\nu \to Cl^\bullet + ClOO^\bullet$, (3) $ClOO^\bullet + M \to Cl^\bullet + O_2 + M$, and (4) $2(Cl^\bullet + O_3 \to ClO^\bullet + O_2)$, yielding the net reaction $2O_3 \to 3O_2$. The rate of ozone loss is governed by: $-\frac{d[O_3]}{dt} = 2k_1[ClO^\bullet]^2[M]$. At a polar altitude where $k_1 = 5.00 \times 10^{-32}\text{ cm}^6\text{ molecule}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$, $[M] = 1.50 \times 10^{18}\text{ molecules cm}^{-3}$, and $[ClO^\bullet] = 1.00 \times 10^{10}\text{ molecules cm}^{-3}$, calculate the instantaneous rate of ozone destruction $-\frac{d[O_3]}{dt}$ in units of $10^6\text{ molecules cm}^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$.
questions.explanation: Applying the rate equation for ozone destruction via the $ClO$ dimer catalytic cycle: $-\frac{d[O_3]}{dt} = 2k_1[ClO^\bullet]^2[M]$. Substituting the specified kinetic rate constant and molecular concentrations: $-\frac{d[O_3]}{dt} = 2 \times (5.00 \times 10^{-32}\text{ cm}^6\text{ molecule}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}) \times (1.00 \times 10^{10}\text{ molecules cm}^{-3})^2 \times (1.50 \times 10^{18}\text{ molecules cm}^{-3})$. Evaluating step-by-step: $(1.00 \times 10^{10})^2 = 1.00 \times 10^{20}\text{ molecules}^2\text{ cm}^{-6}$. Multiplying the constants together yields: $-\frac{d[O_3]}{dt} = 2 \times (5.00 \times 10^{-32}) \times (1.00 \times 10^{20}) \times (1.50 \times 10^{18}) = (1.00 \times 10^{-31}) \times (1.50 \times 10^{38}) = 1.50 \times 10^7\text{ molecules cm}^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$. Expressing this value in units of $10^6\text{ molecules cm}^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$ gives: $\frac{1.50 \times 10^7}{10^6} = 15$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: An industrial green chemistry plant synthesizes a batch of specialty bio-pesticide. The manufacturing process consumes $500\text{ kg}$ of chemical starting reagents, $1250\text{ kg}$ of process solvents, and $250\text{ kg}$ of aqueous extraction agents, yielding $400\text{ kg}$ of pure isolated crystalline product. None of the spent solvents or aqueous phases are recovered or recycled. The Environmental Factor is defined as the ratio of total mass of waste generated to the mass of finished product: $E\text{-factor} = \frac{m_{\text{waste}}}{m_{\text{product}}}$. Calculate the exact numerical value of the $E\text{-factor}$ for this manufacturing run.
questions.explanation: First, applying the law of conservation of mass, the total mass of materials entering the manufacturing process is the sum of all inputs: $m_{\text{input, total}} = m_{\text{reagents}} + m_{\text{solvents}} + m_{\text{aqueous}} = 500 + 1250 + 250 = 2000\text{ kg}$. The mass of the isolated target product is $m_{\text{product}} = 400\text{ kg}$. Since all unrecovered input mass becomes waste, the total waste mass is: $m_{\text{waste}} = m_{\text{input, total}} - m_{\text{product}} = 2000 - 400 = 1600\text{ kg}$. Applying the standard definition of the Environmental Factor ($E\text{-factor}$): $E = \frac{m_{\text{waste}}}{m_{\text{product}}} = \frac{1600\text{ kg}}{400\text{ kg}} = 4$. (Alternatively, Process Mass Intensity is $PMI = \frac{2000}{400} = 5$, and $E = PMI - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4$).
